content: 1. Kohler et al. (2014) evaluated the safety, feasibility, and acceptability of the PrePex device for adult male circumcision in Malawi. Their findings were published in PLoS One. 2. Mavhu et al. (2016) assessed the safety and acceptability of the PrePex device during routine male circumcision service delivery in Zimbabwe under active surveillance. This study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 3. Milovanovic et al. (2016) explored perceptions of the PrePex device among men who either underwent or refused circumcision, as well as their companions. The results were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 4. Musau et al. (2011) investigated the safety profile and acceptability of a disposable male circumcision device among Kenyan men undergoing voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC). Their findings appeared in the Journal of Urology. 5. Musiige et al. (2016) reported on participant experiences and views regarding odor and pain associated with PrePex device removal in a VMMC pilot study conducted in Botswana. The study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 6. Mutabazi et al. (2012) conducted a prospective, randomized, non-masked trial comparing a non-surgical device to a surgical technique for male circumcision in resource-limited settings. Their findings, focused on HIV prevention, were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 7. Sokal et al. (2014) performed a field study on adult male circumcision using the ShangRing device in routine clinical settings in Kenya and Zambia. The results were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 8. Sokal et al. (2014) also conducted a randomized controlled trial comparing the ShangRing device to conventional surgical techniques for adult male circumcision, focusing on safety and acceptability. This study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 9. Tshimanga et al. (2016) evaluated the safety profile of the PrePex device and client satisfaction among adolescent males aged 13–17 years in Zimbabwe. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 10. Tshimanga et al. (2016) conducted a Phase II randomized controlled trial comparing the safety, procedure time, and cost of the PrePex device to forceps-guided surgical circumcision in Zimbabwe. The study was published in PLoS One. 11. Bratt and Zyambo (2013) compared the direct costs of facility-based ShangRing provision versus standard surgical techniques for VMMC in Zambia. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 12. Duffy et al. (2013) evaluated the reach and cost-effectiveness of the PrePex device for safe male circumcision in Uganda. The study was published in PLoS One. 13. Kim et al. (2015) assessed the cost of adult VMMC in a mixed (surgical and PrePex) site compared to a hypothetical PrePex-only site in South Africa. Their findings were published in Global Health Action. 14. Njeuhmeli et al. (2014) conducted a cost analysis of integrating the PrePex device into a VMMC program in Zimbabwe. The study was published in PLoS One. 15. Obiero et al. (2013) concluded that the PrePex device is unlikely to achieve cost savings compared to the forceps-guided method in male circumcision programs in sub-Saharan Africa. Their findings were published in PLoS One. 16. Schutte et al. (2016) performed a comparative cost analysis of surgical and PrePex device male circumcision in Zimbabwe and Mozambique. The results were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 17. Vandament et al. (2016) evaluated opportunities for cost efficiencies through the introduction of PrePex device male circumcision in adult VMMC programs in Zambia and Zimbabwe. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 18. Several studies have explored the acceptability of VMMC among younger adolescent boys (ages 10–14) compared to delaying the procedure until later adolescence (ages ≥15). These studies assessed outcomes such as adequate foreskin removal, cosmesis, psychological distress, pain, inconvenience, complications, procedure time, and time to return to normal activities. Findings suggest that VMMC at younger ages may be acceptable if concerns about pain and procedural care are addressed, particularly given the long-term benefits of HIV prevention. 19. Cost analyses indicate that the timing of VMMC (ages 10–14 vs. ≥15) does not significantly affect resource requirements. However, circumcising younger adolescents may result in higher costs per HIV infection averted due to the delayed onset of sexual activity and associated HIV risk. 20. Feasibility studies highlight the need for adolescent-specific training for VMMC providers, particularly regarding counseling approaches tailored to younger clients. Facility managers and providers emphasized the importance of age-appropriate education and counseling, with younger adolescents receiving less detailed sexual health information compared to older adolescents. 21. Equity considerations suggest that circumcising younger adolescents may be more cost-effective than targeting older males, as the latter group often requires more intensive demand-creation efforts. However, excluding younger adolescents from VMMC programs could have unintended consequences, such as reduced community acceptance and loss of follow-up. 22. Overall, VMMC is a highly cost-effective HIV prevention method with lifetime benefits.
